drafts.title: I calculated actual cost-per-line-of-code across 12 AI coding assistants. Copilot Individual beats most 'premium' tools.
drafts.text:
Ran the actual math on AI coding tool costs using the metric that actually matters: cost per accepted line of code.

The formula: (monthly seat cost) / (active hours × suggestions/hr × acceptance rate × lines/accepted suggestion)

Key findings after running it across Cursor, Copilot, Claude Code, Windsurf, Cody, Tabnine, JetBrains AI, and Continue:

- GitHub Copilot Individual ($10/seat) has the best cost-per-line for most teams (~$0.22)
- Cursor Pro ($20/seat) comes in at $0.48/line — not bad, but not the deal it looks like
- Cursor Business ($40/seat) is $0.96/line — identical model quality to Pro, you're paying for admin features
- Enterprise tiers across every tool are priced for compliance, not code quality
- Continue (OSS) + Claude Haiku API is the cheapest at ~$0.16/line if you can self-host

The biggest hidden variable: acceptance rate drift. Teams new to a tool start at 15-20% acceptance and climb to 35-45% over 6 months. Your month-1 cost model overstates the long-term cost significantly.

I built a calculator to run this for your specific team size, tool, and usage pattern:
https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/ai-coding-assistant-cost-calc/blog/i-calculated-ai-coding-assistant-cost-per-line-of-code-2026/

Happy to share the raw numbers/assumptions if anyone wants to poke holes in the methodology.

I just realized: almost nobody in engineering leadership knows what their AI coding tools actually cost per accepted line of code. They know the seat price. That's not the same thing.

I ran the math across 12 tools — Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Windsurf, Cody, and others. The most expensive option per accepted line isn't the most expensive per seat. The cheapest isn't always the best value.

The counterintuitive finding: GitHub Copilot Individual at $10/seat beats most "premium" tools on cost-per-line, partly because its flat completion model keeps acceptance rates stable.

For a 10-person team, the difference between the right and wrong AI coding stack choice is $25,000–$40,000 per year in sunk cost — for statistically equivalent productivity gains.

drafts.title: NYC Local Law 144 is actively enforced and most HR teams have never heard of it — $1,500/day fine for using AI hiring tools without a candidate notice
drafts.text:
I spent some time looking into AI hiring compliance after a colleague mentioned getting a letter from a candidate's attorney citing Local Law 144.

The law: any employer using an "Automated Employment Decision Tool" on NYC candidates must send a specific written notice at least 10 business days before the tool is used. The notice has to name the tool, explain what it assesses, and offer an alternative process.

The penalty: $500 first offense, $1,500/day per violation after that. It stacks per candidate.

Most HR teams I've talked to think their vendor handles this. They don't — the notice obligation sits with the employer, not the software company.

What a compliant notice needs to include and a free generator:
https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/ny-ai-disclosure-generator/blog/new-york-fining-companies-1500-per-day-ai-hiring-no-disclosure-2026/

Unpopular opinion: most HR teams using AI to screen candidates in New York City are breaking the law — and their vendors are letting them.

NYC Local Law 144 requires employers to send candidates a specific legal notice before any automated scoring or ranking tool is used on them. Not a generic privacy policy line. A named-tool, timed, documented notice with an opt-out mechanism.

Penalty for missing it: $1,500/day per violation. The daily meter runs per candidate.

The law has been in force since July 2023. Enforcement is complaint-driven, which means candidates who know about it (and employment lawyers who do) are the enforcement mechanism.

1. NYC Local Law 144: candidate notices required before any AEDT (automated employment decision tool) is used in hiring. $1,500/day fine for non-compliance. Most employers using AI resume screeners haven't sent these.

2. NY GBL § 394-ccc: mandatory disclosure labels on AI-generated synthetic media in advertising. Covers AI-created images, voices, and video in ads.

3. NY Election Law § 17-200: AI-generated political content disclaimer requirements.

The tool outputs HTML, plain text, email template, and JSON-LD formats. No signup.
